**Judge halts highway widening until more environmental review is done**

A state judge has blocked a planned highway expansion. Transportation officials had argued that the widening was needed to ease worsening congestion and support regional growth.

In a ruling Tuesday, the court ordered agencies to stop all work on the project until they finish additional environmental review. The judge found that planners had not fully accounted for the expansion's effects on air quality, nearby neighborhoods and climate emissions.

The project would have added two lanes to a corridor that commuters and freight traffic use every day. Business groups and local officials backed it, saying it would reduce bottlenecks, shorten travel times and help the regional economy. Construction was expected to begin later this year.

Environmental organizations and community advocates sued. Widening highways often leads to more driving, more pollution and disruption for people who live near the route, they argued. They also said the state transportation agencies relied on outdated assumptions when they concluded the project would benefit the public.

The judge wrote that the state had not shown how it would mitigate the project's environmental harms, or whether alternatives could meet similar goals with less impact. Those alternatives included expanded transit service, carpool incentives and targeted safety improvements.

"The record shows significant unanswered questions about the long-term consequences of this project," the ruling stated. "Those questions must be addressed before irreversible steps are taken."

Transportation officials said they are reviewing the decision and weighing next steps, including a possible appeal. In a statement, the state Department of Transportation said the corridor remains "one of the most congested in the region" and that officials remain committed to finding solutions that improve mobility and safety.

Opponents welcomed the ruling. "This decision recognizes that bigger highways are not the only answer," said a spokesperson for one of the groups that brought the lawsuit. "Communities deserve transportation investments that reduce pollution and give people real alternatives to driving."

Other major highway projects across the country have also met legal and political resistance as cities and states weigh the environmental costs of car-centered planning.

Unless an appeal overturns the decision, planners will have to revisit the environmental analysis before going forward. That could delay construction for months or even years.

**Axolotl**

The **axolotl** (*Ambystoma mexicanum*) is a salamander native to the lake complex beneath the Valley of Mexico, most notably the remnants of Lake Xochimilco near Mexico City. It is widely known for its unusual appearance and its ability to regrow body parts. Unlike many other salamanders, it usually keeps its larval features for life, a condition called neoteny.

Axolotls have a broad head, lidless eyes, a laterally flattened tail, and three pairs of feathery external gills on the sides of the head. Wild animals are usually dark brown or black with mottled markings. Captive-bred varieties include leucistic, albino, golden, and melanoid forms. Adults commonly reach 15 to 30 cm (6 to 12 in), though size varies.

Axolotls normally stay fully aquatic and do not go through complete metamorphosis into a land-dwelling adult. Metamorphosis occurs rarely in nature and can be induced with hormones, but most axolotls keep their gills and other juvenile traits while reaching sexual maturity. They eat worms, insect larvae, crustaceans, mollusks, and small fish, catching prey by suction.

Axolotls can regrow limbs, tails, parts of the spinal cord, skin, and even portions of the heart and brain without extensive scarring. That has made them model organisms in research on regeneration, development, and genetics. They also breed readily in captivity, which suits laboratory use.

Axolotls were once common in the interconnected lakes of the Mexican Basin and had a place in Aztec mythology. The name comes from the Nahuatl word *āxōlōtl*, often linked to the deity Xolotl. The wild population has since declined sharply. Urbanization, water pollution, habitat loss, the drainage of lakes, and invasive fish such as tilapia and carp have all reduced its numbers.

The IUCN Red List classifies the axolotl as Critically Endangered. Conservation work has centered on restoring habitat in Xochimilco, captive breeding programs, and creating refuges free of invasive species. Captive axolotls remain abundant, however, and are popular in the pet trade and in public aquaria.

# Inkwell 2.0 Release Notes

Inkwell 2.0 redesigns the interface, adds new ways to organize your notes, and makes the app faster and more reliable.

## What's New

**Redesigned interface**
Inkwell has a new look: a cleaner layout, refined typography, and a distraction-free writing mode. Dark mode follows your system settings automatically. There are also six new accent colors.

**Linked notes and Graph View**
Type `[[` to link to any note. The new Graph View shows how your notes relate, which helps you spot patterns and find old ideas again. Backlinks appear at the bottom of each note.

**Real-time collaboration**
Share a note or a whole notebook with teammates, friends, or family. You get live cursors, inline comments, and version history for reviewing changes. Permissions can be set to view, comment, or edit.

**Smart search**
Search is up to three times faster and understands natural language, so queries like "meeting notes from last March" or "photos with handwritten text" work. It also searches text inside images and PDFs.

**Templates and Quick Capture**
There are 25 built-in templates, including daily journal, project plan, and weekly review, and you can create your own. The new Quick Capture widget and shortcut (`Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + N`) let you jot down a thought without opening the full app.

## Improvements

- Markdown support now includes tables, footnotes, and task lists with due dates.
- Notes export to PDF, Markdown, or HTML with formatting preserved.
- Sync is more reliable. Edits made offline on multiple devices are resolved automatically when they conflict.
- Handwriting input on tablets has lower latency and better palm rejection.
- A guided import tool now brings in notes from other note apps.
- App launch is 40% faster on mobile devices.

## Fixes

- Large notebooks no longer slow down scrolling.
- Images no longer appear rotated after syncing.
- Fixed a rare crash when pasting formatted text from web pages.
- Tags no longer disappear when you rename a notebook.
- Screen reader support is better throughout the app.

## Security and privacy

All notes are now end-to-end encrypted by default. You can also lock individual notes with a passcode or biometric authentication.

## Upgrading

Your existing notes migrate automatically the first time you open Inkwell 2.0. We recommend backing up your data first under **Settings > Backup**. The legacy folder system has been replaced by notebooks and tags, and your folders are converted for you.

## Thank you

Many of these features came directly from your feedback. Keep sending it to feedback@inkwell.app. Happy writing!

*The Inkwell Team*

# History of the bicycle

The **history of the bicycle** covers more than two centuries, from a wooden, foot-propelled machine to the lightweight designs used worldwide today.

## Early precursors

The earliest widely recognized ancestor of the bicycle is the *Laufmaschine* ("running machine"), invented by German baron Karl von Drais and first demonstrated in 1817. Also called the draisine or "dandy horse," it had two in-line wheels joined by a wooden frame and a steerable front wheel, but no pedals. The rider sat astride and pushed against the ground with their feet. It was briefly popular among the European upper classes and faded after a few years, partly because of poor road surfaces and bans on riding it on sidewalks.

## Pedals and the velocipede

In the 1860s, French inventors including Pierre Michaux and Pierre Lallement are credited with attaching cranks and pedals directly to the front wheel. The "velocipede" this produced was nicknamed the "boneshaker" for its rigid iron-and-wood construction and rough ride. It set off a short-lived craze across Europe and North America.

## High-wheelers

In the 1870s, designers enlarged the front wheel to go faster, since each pedal revolution covered a distance proportional to the wheel's diameter. The "penny-farthing," or high-wheel bicycle, was popularized by manufacturers such as James Starley in Britain. Metal frames, solid rubber tires, and wire-spoked wheels improved performance. The high seat, though, made falls dangerous, and the bicycle appealed mostly to young, athletic men.

## The safety bicycle

The "safety bicycle" came next. In 1885, John Kemp Starley introduced the Rover, with two wheels of similar size and a chain drive to the rear wheel. Its lower seat made it more stable and accessible. The pneumatic tire, developed by John Boyd Dunlop in 1888, improved comfort and speed. By the 1890s, the "bicycle boom" had made cycling popular across social classes. Cycling also increased women's social mobility and independence, and it influenced changes in clothing.

## Twentieth century and beyond

In the early 1900s, the freewheel, derailleur gears, and lighter alloys made bicycles more versatile. The rise of the automobile reduced cycling's role in transportation in many wealthy countries, but bicycles remained essential in much of Asia, Africa, and Europe. The 1970s brought a fitness-driven boom, and the mountain bike, invented in California that decade, created a new category. Later developments include carbon-fiber frames, electric-assist models, and bike-sharing systems, and interest in cycling as sustainable urban transport has renewed.

# Troubleshooting your home Wi-Fi mesh system

## 1. Start with the basics

Many mesh problems disappear after a simple restart. Unplug the main router and all satellite nodes, wait 30 seconds, then plug in the main router first. Once its light shows a stable status, power on the satellites one at a time.

## 2. Check the internet source

Connect a laptop directly to your modem with an Ethernet cable. If the internet is slow or absent there, the problem is with your provider or modem, not the mesh. Restart the modem and contact your ISP if the issue persists.

## 3. Identify the problem node

Open your mesh app and check each node's status. A node showing a warning or weak connection is the likely culprit. Note which rooms have dropouts, since they point to the faulty or poorly placed unit.

## 4. Fix node placement

Poor placement causes many mesh complaints.

- **Distance:** Place satellites about halfway between the main router and the dead zone, not inside it.
- **Height:** Keep nodes elevated on shelves or tables, not on the floor.
- **Obstructions:** Avoid metal objects, cabinets, and thick concrete walls.
- **Interference:** Keep them away from microwaves, cordless phones, baby monitors, and aquariums.

## 5. Use wired backhaul if you can

If your home has Ethernet cabling, connect the satellites to the main router with cables. This frees up wireless bandwidth and improves speed and stability.

## 6. Update the firmware

Outdated firmware can cause random disconnects and slow speeds. Open the app and check for updates. Most systems can update automatically, so turn that setting on if it's available.

## 7. Check for device-specific issues

If only one device struggles, the mesh may not be at fault. Forget the network on that device and reconnect. Update the device's operating system and Wi-Fi drivers too. Older devices can have trouble switching between nodes, so moving closer to a node may help.

## 8. Reduce channel congestion

In crowded apartment buildings, neighboring networks can interfere. Use your app's channel optimization feature, or switch to a less crowded channel by hand. Putting nearby devices on the 5 GHz band also helps.

## 9. Review connected devices

Too many devices streaming or downloading at once can strain bandwidth. Check your app for bandwidth-heavy devices, and use Quality of Service settings to prioritize video calls or work computers.

## 10. Factory reset, as a last resort

# Council Approves Citywide Bike-Lane Network in Split Vote After Marathon Meeting

**Plan passes 5-4 following five hours of public testimony; construction to begin in spring**

RIVERTON — After a contentious five-hour session that stretched past midnight, the Riverton City Council voted 5-4 Tuesday night to approve a $38 million network of protected bike lanes spanning 42 miles of city streets.

The plan, known as the Riverton Connects Initiative, will build physical barriers between cyclists and traffic along major corridors, including Main Street, Delancey Avenue, and the Harbor Road waterfront. Construction is scheduled to begin in April and conclude within four years.

More than 120 residents signed up to speak, filling the council chamber and an overflow room. Supporters wore green stickers reading "Safe Streets Now," while opponents carried signs warning of lost parking and business disruption.

"My daughter bikes to school, and every morning I hold my breath," said Maria Okafor, a nurse who lives on the east side. "We have lost three cyclists on these roads in five years. This is not abstract for us."

Opponents argued the plan would hurt small businesses by removing roughly 600 on-street parking spaces. Tom Hendricks, who owns a hardware store on Main Street, said his customers need to load heavy materials directly into their vehicles.

"I'm not against bikes," Hendricks told the council. "I'm against being told my business has to absorb the cost of an experiment."

Councilmember Dana Whitfield, who sponsored the measure, said the city had adjusted the proposal in response to concerns. Revisions included preserving loading zones near commercial districts and adding 250 off-street parking spaces in underused municipal lots.

"No plan will satisfy everyone," Whitfield said before the vote. "But doing nothing has a cost too, and we have been paying it in injuries and congestion."

Councilmember Robert Vance, who led the opposition, criticized the price tag and the pace of the rollout. "We are committing tens of millions of dollars while our water mains are failing," he said. "Residents deserve better prioritization."

An amendment from Vance that would have required a one-year pilot program before full approval failed 5-4, with the same members on each side.

Roughly 60 percent of the funding will come from state and federal transportation grants, with the remainder drawn from a municipal bond approved by voters in 2021.

Mayor Elaine Cho said she would sign the ordinance this week. The city will hold a series of neighborhood meetings in February to finalize design details for each corridor.

Outside City Hall after the vote, Okafor said, "It's a start." Hendricks was blunter: "This isn't over."

**State University Announces Free Tuition Program for Low-Income Students**

State University said Tuesday it will offer free tuition to undergraduates from low-income families. School leaders say the goal is to widen access to college and reduce student debt.

Starting in the fall semester next year, students whose families earn $75,000 or less a year will qualify, according to university officials. The program will cover the full cost of tuition after federal and state grants are applied. Students may still owe for housing, meals, and books.

University President Maria Ellis called the plan a "transformational investment" in students and the broader community.

"No talented student should feel that a college education is out of reach because of cost," Ellis said at a campus news conference. "This program sends a clear message: if you have the ability and the drive to succeed, we will do everything we can to make that possible."

The university expects the program to benefit nearly 4,000 current and incoming students each year. Funding will come from endowment earnings, private donations, and a reallocation of institutional financial aid resources. Officials said the school recently completed a fundraising campaign that exceeded its goals, which helped make the initiative possible.

The announcement comes as colleges across the country face pressure to address affordability. Tuition has climbed steadily over the past decade, and many families worry about taking on debt. Advocates have pushed institutions with strong finances to expand need-based aid.

Students on campus welcomed the news as a major step toward easing financial stress. "This could change everything for families like mine," said sophomore Jasmine Carter, who works part-time while attending classes. "A lot of students are balancing school with jobs just to stay enrolled."

Eligibility will be based on financial information submitted through standard aid applications. The school also plans to expand advising and academic support for students in the program, aiming to improve retention and graduation rates.

Some policy experts praised the initiative but said covering tuition alone may not remove every barrier. Living expenses often make up a large share of college costs, especially for students from lower-income households.

Applications will open later this year alongside the university's regular admissions and financial aid process. Officials said more details, including income verification requirements and renewal criteria, will be published on the university's website in the coming weeks.

City Council Approves 22-Mile Bike-Lane Network on 5-4 Vote

The City Council on Tuesday approved a network of protected bike lanes by a 5-4 vote, ending months of public debate and a meeting that ran late into the evening. Officials and residents were split over cost, traffic impacts and public safety.

The plan calls for roughly 22 miles of new protected bike lanes, upgrades to key intersections, improved signage and more bike parking near business districts, schools and transit hubs. City transportation officials said the network is meant to connect neighborhoods that now lack safe cycling infrastructure and to give cyclists continuous routes from downtown to the north, west and riverfront areas.

Supporters said it would reduce traffic congestion, lower emissions and make streets safer for cyclists and pedestrians.

“This is about giving people more options for how they move around the city,” Council President Maria Alvarez said after the vote. “For years, residents have asked for a transportation system that is safer, more modern and less dependent on cars. Tonight, we acted on that.”

Residents, business owners and advocacy groups testified for hours before the vote. Opponents argued that the project would eliminate too many on-street parking spaces and worsen traffic on corridors that are already crowded. Several business owners warned that construction could disrupt commerce and reduce customer access.

“This plan moves too fast and asks neighborhoods to shoulder too much of the burden,” said Councilmember James Porter, who voted against the measure. “We all want safer streets, but this proposal needed more revision and stronger protections for local businesses.”

The room was divided the way the community is. After the final vote, cycling advocates wearing reflective stickers rang bicycle bells. Critics left frustrated, saying the council had ignored practical concerns in favor of a political statement.

Construction will begin early next year in three phases. The first work will go to corridors where city data show higher rates of bicycle and pedestrian crashes. Officials said funding will come from local capital funds, state transportation grants and federal infrastructure dollars.

Mayor Elaine Brooks, who has strongly backed the initiative, said she would sign the measure later this week. In a statement, she called the network “an investment in safety, mobility and the city’s future.”

# Great Molasses Flood

The **Great Molasses Flood**, also known as the **Boston Molasses Disaster**, occurred on January 15, 1919, in the North End neighborhood of Boston, Massachusetts. A large storage tank filled with molasses burst, sending a wave of molasses through the streets. The flood killed 21 people and injured about 150.

## Background

The tank belonged to the Purity Distilling Company, a subsidiary of the United States Industrial Alcohol Company (USIA). It stood about 50 feet (15 m) tall and 90 feet (27 m) in diameter, and held roughly 2.3 million US gallons of molasses. The molasses was brought by ship from the Caribbean and fermented into industrial alcohol, which was used in the manufacture of munitions. It was also used in the production of rum.

The tank was completed in 1915 and was poorly built. The steel was thinner than the tank's size required, and it was never tested by being filled with water. It leaked from the start, and the company reportedly painted it brown to hide the leakage rather than fix the problem. Residents collected leaking molasses from the base of the tank.

## Disaster

On the day of the disaster, temperatures in Boston had risen sharply, from about 2 °F (−17 °C) to above 40 °F (4 °C). Shortly after noon, the tank ruptured. Witnesses described a loud rumbling and the sound of rivets popping like machine-gun fire. A wave of molasses estimated at up to 25 feet (7.6 m) high at its crest moved through the streets at around 35 miles per hour (56 km/h).

The wave destroyed buildings, damaged the elevated railway structure, and swept up people, horses, and vehicles. Most of the dead were killed by drowning or by injuries from debris. Rescue was difficult because the thick, cooling molasses trapped victims.

## Aftermath

Boston firefighters, police, Red Cross workers, and sailors from the USS *Nantucket* helped with rescue and cleanup. Cleanup took weeks, and the harbor remained brown with molasses into the summer.

Residents filed one of the earliest major class-action lawsuits in Massachusetts against USIA. The company claimed that anarchists had sabotaged the tank, but an auditor appointed by the court, Hugh W. Ogden, concluded after hearing years of testimony that the tank's structural design was inadequate. In 1925, USIA was ordered to pay damages, and settlements totaled roughly $600,000. The case contributed to stricter building regulations and to the requirement that engineers and architects sign off on construction plans.

## Legacy

A plaque commemorates the disaster near the site, now a park and playground. A popular legend holds that the neighborhood smells of molasses on hot summer days. # Trans-Siberian Railway

The **Trans-Siberian Railway** (Russian: Транссибирская магистраль, *Transsibirskaya magistral*) is a network of railway lines connecting European Russia with the Russian Far East. It runs about 9,289 kilometres (5,772 miles) between Moscow and Vladivostok and is the longest continuous railway line in the world. The route crosses eight time zones and passes through more than 80 cities and towns.

## History

Construction began in 1891 under Tsar Alexander III. Tsarevich Nicholas, later Nicholas II, ceremonially inaugurated the work at Vladivostok. The government wanted to tighten its hold on the eastern territories, encourage settlement and trade, and move troops more easily in the Far East. Finance minister Sergei Witte advocated and organized the project.

Thousands of laborers built the line: soldiers, convicts, and hired workers. They dealt with permafrost, rough terrain, harsh winters, and long distances. Most main sections were complete by 1904. The Circum-Baikal section around Lake Baikal was finished later, and until then passengers crossed the lake by ferry. During the Russo-Japanese War (1904–1905), the line's limited capacity hampered Russian supply efforts.

## Route

The principal route runs from Moscow eastward through Nizhny Novgorod, Yekaterinburg, Omsk, Novosibirsk, Krasnoyarsk, Irkutsk, Ulan-Ude, Chita, and Khabarovsk before reaching Vladivostok on the Pacific coast. Along the way it crosses the Ural Mountains and the Ob and Yenisei rivers, and it follows the shores of Lake Baikal, the world's deepest lake.

Several branches leave the main line. The Trans-Mongolian route diverges near Ulan-Ude and goes through Mongolia to Beijing, while the Trans-Manchurian route enters northeastern China via Harbin. The later Baikal–Amur Mainline (BAM) runs as a northern alternative through eastern Siberia.

## Operation

Russian Railways operates the line, which is fully electrified and double-tracked. It carries a large share of Russia's freight, including coal, timber, oil products, and containers moving between Asia and Europe. Container traffic has made it a competitor to maritime shipping routes for some goods.

Passenger service continues. The Moscow–Vladivostok journey takes about six to seven days on the long-distance train *Rossiya*. Tourists also ride the line for the Siberian landscapes and the experience of long-distance rail travel.

## Cultural impact

The railway appears in literature, film, and travel writing, often as a symbol of Russia's size and of overland journeys.

- Baikal–Amur Mainline
- Rail transport in Russia

# Microplastics found in most tap and bottled water samples, new study reports

*Researchers say filtration could cut particle levels significantly, but health effects remain unclear*

A new multi-country study found microplastic particles in the large majority of drinking water samples it tested. The result renews questions about how the fragments move through the water supply and what they might mean for human health.

The research, published this week in the journal *Environmental Science Advances*, analyzed more than 1,200 samples of tap water, bottled water, and household-filtered water from 14 countries. Microplastics turned up in 87 percent of them. Bottled water had the highest average concentration, roughly twice the level in municipal tap water.

"We expected to find them, but we didn't expect them to be so consistent across regions and water sources," said Dr. Elena Marchetti, the study's lead author. "Microplastics are now part of the background of our water systems."

## Where the particles come from

The team used spectroscopy to identify the particles. Polyethylene, polypropylene, and polyester fibers were the most common. The researchers say likely sources include degraded packaging, synthetic textiles shed during washing, tire dust, and aging plumbing. In bottled water, they linked many particles to the bottles and caps, which can shed fragments through repeated opening or exposure to heat.

The study also looked at particles smaller than one micrometer, often called nanoplastics. These are harder to detect and may be more biologically active. The authors measured them with less certainty, but estimate they may outnumber larger fragments by a wide margin.

## What helps

Water treated with reverse osmosis or multi-stage carbon block filters had particle counts about 70 to 90 percent lower than unfiltered samples. Boiling and filtering through a fine mesh also reduced particle levels in some tests, though results varied.

## Health questions remain

The authors stressed that the study did not assess health outcomes. Scientists still don't know what level of microplastic exposure, if any, poses a risk. Some laboratory studies suggest the particles could trigger inflammation or carry harmful chemicals, but evidence in humans is limited.

"People shouldn't panic, but this isn't something to dismiss either," said Dr. Raj Patel, an environmental toxicologist not involved in the research. "We need standardized testing methods and long-term studies to understand what these exposures mean."

The authors are calling for international monitoring standards and more investment in treatment technology. Several regulators have begun reviewing guidelines, but most countries have no binding limits for microplastics in drinking water.

# Ferry Service Returns to Harbor Island After Two-Year Absence

**PORT MARLOWE —** The *Marguerite* pulled into Port Marlowe on Monday morning to a chorus of horns and cheers, the first passenger ferry from the mainland to Harbor Island in two years.

More than 300 residents gathered along the waterfront to watch the 140-foot vessel complete its first scheduled crossing since service was halted in the spring of 2022. Some waved homemade banners. Others stood quietly, hands over their mouths, as the ramp lowered onto the dock.

"I've waited a long time to see that boat come in," said Eleanor Briggs, 78, who has lived on the island for six decades. "Two years of arranging rides on fishing boats and begging favors from neighbors. It's been exhausting."

Service was suspended after an inspection found structural corrosion in the vessel that had served the route for nearly 40 years. Officials first projected a six-month interruption. Delays in securing replacement funding, along with supply chain problems and a shipyard backlog, stretched it to two years.

The *Marguerite* was bought last year from a retired Scandinavian route and refitted for $14.2 million. It carries 180 passengers and 22 vehicles. The state transportation department paid roughly 70 percent of the cost, and county funds and a federal rural transit grant covered the rest.

Transportation Director Alan Pruitt called the ferry's return "a long-overdue lifeline."

"This isn't just a boat," Pruitt said at the dockside ceremony. "It's how people get to work, how kids get to school, how patients reach the hospital. Its absence was felt in every part of island life."

Harbor Island's population dropped an estimated 11 percent, according to county figures, and at least four small businesses closed. Tourism, the island's main industry, fell by more than half in the first year.

Local innkeeper Tomás Reyes said he nearly sold his business. "We had maybe a dozen bookings all last summer," he said. "Now my phone hasn't stopped ringing. I've got reservations through September."

The ferry will make six round trips daily in summer, with a reduced schedule in winter. Adult fares are $12 and standard vehicles are $38, with discounted rates for island residents.

Captain Dana Whitfield, who piloted the first crossing, said the crew felt the moment too. "We could see people lining the shore from a mile out," she said. "It gave me chills."

The next departure was scheduled for 11:30 a.m. It sold out within the hour.

# Rosetta Stone

The **Rosetta Stone** is a fragment of a granodiorite stele inscribed with a decree issued at Memphis, Egypt, in 196 BC during the Ptolemaic dynasty on behalf of King Ptolemy V Epiphanes. The decree appears in three scripts: Ancient Egyptian hieroglyphs, Demotic script, and Ancient Greek. Because the same text appears in all three, the stone made modern understanding of Egyptian hieroglyphs possible. It is held in the British Museum in London, where it has been on near-continuous display since 1802 and is one of the museum's most visited objects.

## Discovery

French soldiers found the stone on 15 July 1799 during Napoleon Bonaparte's Egyptian campaign. Lieutenant Pierre-François Bouchard, who was strengthening defenses near the town of Rashid (Rosetta) in the Nile Delta, saw that the slab might be important. It was probably first displayed in a temple, possibly at Sais, then moved in the medieval period and reused as building material.

After the French defeat in Egypt, the stone passed to British forces under the Treaty of Alexandria (1801). It was transported to England and presented to the British Museum in 1802. Egypt has since asked for its return.

## Content

The decree, issued by a council of priests, affirms the royal cult of the 13-year-old Ptolemy V on the first anniversary of his coronation. It lists the benefactions the king had granted to temples and priests, such as tax reductions, and details his suppression of rebellions. It also orders that copies of the decree be placed in temples throughout the country. The Rosetta Stone is believed to be one of these copies.

## Decipherment

Scholars understood Greek well, so the Greek portion gave them an immediate way into the other texts. Silvestre de Sacy and Johan David Åkerblad made early progress by identifying some names and words in the Demotic text. Thomas Young, an English polymath, showed that the cartouches in the hieroglyphic text enclosed royal names such as Ptolemy.

Jean-François Champollion announced his decipherment in 1822. Building on the earlier work and drawing on his knowledge of Coptic, he showed that hieroglyphs combined phonetic signs with ideographic elements. This made it possible to read Egyptian inscriptions and papyri.

## Legacy

The phrase "Rosetta Stone" is now used for a key clue to a new field of knowledge. It is also the name of a language-learning software brand and of the European Space Agency's Rosetta space probe.

- Egyptian hieroglyphs
- Jean-François Champollion
- Ptolemaic Kingdom

# Eleven Notebooks in a Shoebox

In the back of my closet, in a shoebox that once held winter boots, there are eleven notebooks. Some have cracked spines and coffee rings. One has a lock, and I lost the key in 2009. I haven't read most of them since I wrote them, and I still can't throw them away. If I never reread them, what are they for?

I think a journal serves the person writing it, not whoever might read it later. When I'm tangled in a worry, it's a fog, shapeless and large. Writing it down forces me to pick words. I have to decide what happened, what I feel, and which of the two is bothering me. The fog becomes a sentence, and a sentence can be looked at. About half the time, by the end of the page, the problem has shrunk to its real size. The rest of the time it has grown, and I finally see why I've been so tired.

Most of our days go unseen. The small humiliation in a meeting, the odd joy of a light-filled kitchen, the thought that arrived at a red light and then evaporated: nobody catches those. Friends can't hear everything, and they shouldn't have to. A journal never gets bored and never steers the conversation toward itself. It takes everything in, and that's a relief.

Memory edits badly. It smooths rough years into tidy stories and forgets how uncertain we were while living them. Last spring I opened an old notebook and found myself at twenty-six, sure that a job rejection had ruined my life. I had no memory of that despair. I only remembered the better thing that came after. I felt tender toward that anxious person, and I took away some humility too: what I'm sure is a catastrophe today may be a forgotten footnote next year.

Journals can be vain, too. I've caught myself writing as if a biographer were reading over my shoulder, polishing a sentence so I'd sound wiser than I was. Even that tells me something, though. The self I perform on the page is the one I hope to become.

I also write to pay attention. Days move too fast to leave room for reflection, and a notebook is a small way of saying this day happened and I was here. The entries needn't be profound. "Rained all day. Made soup. Called Mom." Years later, lines like that bring a whole day back.

So the notebooks stay in the shoebox. I may never read them again, and that's fine. The work was done when I wrote them, when I turned the blur of living into something I could hold. Tonight I'll probably add another page.

# Hildegard of Bingen

**Hildegard of Bingen** (German: *Hildegard von Bingen*; Latin: *Hildegardis Bingensis*; 1098 – 17 September 1179), also known as **Saint Hildegard** and the **Sibyl of the Rhine**, was a German Benedictine abbess, writer, mystic, naturalist, and composer. She is among the best-documented figures in medieval music, and one of the earliest composers whose life and works are well preserved.

## Early life

Hildegard was born around 1098 in Bermersheim, in the Rhineland, to a noble family. According to tradition, she was the tenth child and was offered to the Church as a tithe. From about the age of eight she was educated at the Disibodenberg monastery under the anchoress Jutta of Sponheim. Hildegard reported visions from early childhood. After Jutta died in 1136, she was elected leader of the women's community.

## Religious career

Around 1150, Hildegard moved her community to a new convent at Rupertsberg, near Bingen, and later founded a second house at Eibingen. Pope Eugenius III reviewed and approved her visionary writings in 1147–48, which raised her authority. She corresponded with popes, emperors, and other leaders, among them Bernard of Clairvaux and Frederick Barbarossa. She also went on several preaching tours, which was unusual for a woman of her time.

## Musical works

More of Hildegard's music survives than of any other medieval composer of chant. About seventy-five compositions are extant, mostly in the *Dendermonde* and *Riesencodex* manuscripts. Her best-known work is the *Ordo Virtutum* ("Play of the Virtues"), a morality play set to music and one of the earliest surviving examples of liturgical drama. Her other major collection is the *Symphonia armonie celestium revelationum* ("Symphony of the Harmony of Celestial Revelations"), a cycle of antiphons, responsories, sequences, and hymns honoring saints, the Virgin Mary, and the Holy Spirit.

Her melodies are monophonic. They cover a wide range, with large leaps and long melismatic lines, unlike the narrower contours of typical Gregorian chant.

## Other writings

Hildegard's major visionary works include *Scivias* (c. 1151), *Liber vitae meritorum*, and *Liber divinorum operum*. She also wrote the natural-history and medical texts *Physica* and *Causae et curae*, and invented a constructed language, the *Lingua ignota*.

## Legacy

Hildegard died at Rupertsberg in 1179. Interest in her music revived in the late 20th century, and recordings of it reached wide audiences. She had been venerated as a saint for centuries before Pope Benedict XVI formally canonized her in 2012 and named her a Doctor of the Church. Her feast day is 17 September.

# Axolotl

The **axolotl** (*Ambystoma mexicanum*) is a paedomorphic salamander native to the lake complex of Xochimilco near Mexico City. Unlike most amphibians, it reaches adulthood without undergoing metamorphosis, retaining its aquatic larval features, including external gills and a dorsal tailfin, throughout its life. It is used in scientific research and kept as a pet, but it is critically endangered in the wild.

## Etymology

The name derives from the Nahuatl word *āxōlōtl*, often translated as "water dog" or "water monster." It is associated with Xolotl, the Aztec god of fire and lightning, who according to legend transformed himself into an axolotl to escape sacrifice.

## Description

Adults typically measure 15–45 cm in length, though most are around 23 cm. The head is broad, with a wide mouth, small lidless eyes, and three pairs of feathery external gills that extend from behind the head. Wild-type axolotls are dark brown or olive with gold speckling, but captive populations show several color variants, including leucistic (pale pink with black eyes), albino, golden, and melanoid forms. Axolotls have four limbs, with four toes on the front feet and five on the hind feet, and they have both gills and rudimentary lungs.

## Habitat and ecology

Axolotls are native only to Lake Xochimilco and, historically, Lake Chalco. They prefer cold, clean, deep water, generally between 14 and 20 °C. They are carnivorous, feeding on worms, insect larvae, small fish, mollusks, and crustaceans, which they locate by smell and capture by suction. Sexual maturity is reached at roughly 18 to 24 months. Females lay hundreds of eggs, which are attached individually to aquatic plants.

## Regeneration

The axolotl can regrow entire limbs, parts of the heart and brain, the spinal cord, and the tail, usually without scarring. This has made it a model organism in developmental biology, regenerative medicine, and cancer research. Its genome, sequenced in 2018, is about ten times larger than the human genome, among the largest sequenced to date.

## Metamorphosis

Neoteny in axolotls results from low levels of thyroid hormone. Metamorphosis can be artificially induced by injecting thyroxine or iodine, producing a lung-breathing, terrestrial form resembling the tiger salamander, though this often shortens the animal's lifespan.

## Conservation status

The axolotl is listed as **critically endangered** by the IUCN. Wild populations have declined sharply because of urban expansion, water pollution, draining of lakes, and the introduction of invasive fish such as tilapia and carp. Surveys in the early 21st century suggested only a few hundred individuals remained in the wild. Conservation efforts include habitat restoration, the creation of traditional *chinampa* refuges, and captive breeding programs.

## Cultural significance

The axolotl appears in Mexican art and folklore and is featured on the 50-peso banknote. It also appears in video games and other popular media.

## Home Wi-Fi mesh troubleshooting guide

A Wi-Fi mesh system uses several nodes to spread wireless coverage through your home. If the internet is slow, devices keep dropping, or some rooms get a weak signal, work through this checklist.

### 1. Check the basics
Start with the simple things:
- Make sure your modem and main mesh router are powered on.
- Confirm every mesh node has power and shows a normal status light.
- If you can, plug a device straight into the modem to confirm the internet service itself is working.
- Restart the whole system: modem first, then the main router, then the mesh nodes.

A full reboot often clears temporary connection problems.

### 2. Confirm node placement
Spacing matters for mesh nodes.
- Place the main router in a central, open spot.
- Put nodes about halfway between the main router and the weak-signal areas.
- Avoid cabinets, the backs of TVs, thick walls, metal objects, microwaves, and cordless phones.
- A node placed too far out connects poorly and can drag down the whole network.

Each node needs a strong signal from the previous node before it can extend coverage farther.

### 3. Check for overcrowding
Too many connected devices can slow the network, especially when several are streaming, gaming, or downloading large files at once.
- Disconnect devices you aren't using.
- Pause heavy downloads and test again.
- If your mesh app supports it, look for the devices using the most bandwidth.

Some systems also let you prioritize traffic for work calls or gaming.

### 4. Update firmware
Outdated firmware can cause instability, slow speeds, and security risks.
- Open the mesh system's app or web portal.
- Check for firmware updates on the main router and on every node.
- Install the updates and let the system restart fully.

Turn on automatic updates if your system offers them.

### 5. Test speed in the right places
Run a speed test in three places:
- Near the main router
- Near each mesh node
- In the room where performance is poor

If speed is good at the main router but bad near a node, the problem is usually node placement or interference.

### 6. Reduce wireless interference
Nearby devices competing for the same signal space can slow Wi-Fi down.
- Move nodes away from baby monitors, Bluetooth hubs, cordless phone bases, and microwave ovens.
- Use the 5 GHz band for speed when you're close to a node.
- Use 2.4 GHz for longer range or older devices.

Many mesh systems pick bands automatically, but placement still matters.

### 7. Reset as a last resort
If a node won't connect or its settings seem corrupted:
- Remove the node from the app.
- Factory reset it with the reset button.
- Add it back to the mesh network.

If problems continue after all these steps, contact your internet provider or the mesh system's support team. Have your model number, firmware version, and a description of the problem ready.

Trans-Siberian Railway

The Trans-Siberian Railway is the longest railway line in the world. It runs across Russia from Moscow in the west to Vladivostok on the Pacific coast. The main route is about 9,289 kilometres (5,772 miles) long and crosses eight time zones, with a wide range of landscapes and climates along the way.

Construction began in 1891 under Tsar Alexander III. His son, the future Nicholas II, marked the start with a ceremony in Vladivostok. Thousands of labourers, soldiers, and convicts built the line in sections, in difficult terrain and weather. By 1916 a continuous rail connection ran from European Russia to the Pacific. The Amur Railway made that possible, because it let the route stay entirely within Russian territory.

The imperial government built the line for strategic and economic reasons. It strengthened control over the distant eastern territories and encouraged migration to Siberia, and it served trade and resource extraction. The line was of great military and logistical value during the Russian Civil War and the Soviet period. Through the 20th century it carried goods, people, and raw materials.

Several routes are linked to the Trans-Siberian system. The Trans-Mongolian Railway runs from Ulan-Ude through Mongolia to Beijing, and the Trans-Manchurian Railway passes through northeastern China. The Baikal–Amur Mainline (BAM) was built farther north in the Soviet era as an alternative to the main route.

Major cities on the line include Yekaterinburg, Omsk, Novosibirsk, Krasnoyarsk, Irkutsk, Ulan-Ude, Khabarovsk, and Vladivostok. It also passes near Lake Baikal, the world's deepest freshwater lake. Much of the line has since been electrified, which raised its efficiency and capacity.

The railway is also a symbol of Russia's vastness, and it appears in literature, journalism, film, and tourism. Long-distance passenger journeys on it are known internationally for their length and for the experience of crossing Eurasia by rail.

Today the Trans-Siberian remains a key part of Russia's transport infrastructure.

**Ferry Service Resumes After Two-Year Suspension**

The ferry between Harbor Point and Seaview Island resumed operations on Monday, two years after it stopped running. Thousands of residents along the coast had been without it.

The route was halted in 2024 after storms badly damaged port infrastructure, and safety upgrades followed. Commuters, business owners and local officials welcomed its return, saying the region relies on it for both its economy and its social life.

The first sailing left shortly after 7 a.m. with passengers, vehicles and freight, the first crossing in nearly 24 months. Small crowds gathered at both terminals to watch the vessel depart and arrive. Many passengers said the resumption showed the area was recovering.

"This ferry is more than transportation — it's a lifeline," said Mayor Elena Brooks at a reopening ceremony at Harbor Point. "For two years, families, workers, and businesses have had to rely on longer, more expensive alternatives. Today marks an important step forward."

During the suspension, travelers had to drive a detour of more than 80 miles or depend on limited private boat services. Tourism operators, restaurants and suppliers said the closure raised their costs and cut the number of visitors during peak seasons.

Port authorities said significant repairs and modernization work at both terminals was finished before the route reopened. It included reinforced docking facilities, upgraded passenger waiting areas, and new navigation and safety systems meant to make the crossing more reliable in poor weather.

The ferry operator, Coastal Transit, said it will run three round trips daily at first and expand to a full timetable by the summer if demand remains strong. Tickets went on sale last month, and the company called early bookings from residents and tourists "encouraging."

# Backend team onboarding guide

This guide covers your first three months on the backend team.

## Week one: get set up

**Access and tools:** Your manager will request access to the code repositories, CI/CD pipelines, cloud console, monitoring dashboards, and communication channels. If anything is still missing on day two, ask in the team channel instead of waiting.

**Local environment:** Clone the main service repository and follow the README to run the application locally. By the end of the week, the test suite should pass on your machine. If the setup docs are wrong or out of date, fix them in a pull request. It makes a good first contribution.

**People:** You'll be paired with an onboarding buddy, who answers questions, reviews your early work, and explains the team's unwritten conventions. Also schedule one-on-ones with your manager, tech lead, and product partner.

## Weeks two and three: learn the system

**Architecture:** Read the architecture overview and service diagrams. Work out how requests flow through the system, where data lives, and which services depend on each other. Then draw your own diagram and have your buddy correct it.

**Codebase tour:** Explore the code with a specific task in mind: trace one API request from the entry point to the database and back. That teaches more than reading code at random.

**First ticket:** Pick up a small, well-scoped issue tagged "good first issue" and aim to ship it to production by the end of week three. You are walking the full path once: branch, review, merge, deploy, verify.

## Weeks four to six: take on more

**Observability:** Learn to read logs, metrics, and traces so you know where to look when something breaks. Shadow an on-call engineer for at least one rotation before taking your own.

**Code reviews:** Start reviewing teammates' pull requests. Fresh eyes catch things veterans miss, and reviewing is one of the fastest ways to learn the codebase.

**Larger work:** Take on a medium-sized feature or bug with your buddy's guidance. Write a short design note first so the team can give feedback early.

## Working norms

- **Ask early:** If you've been stuck for more than 30 minutes, ask for help.
- **Write things down:** Document decisions and discoveries so the next person doesn't have to rediscover them.
- **Keep changes small:** Small pull requests are easier to review and safer to deploy.
- **Test your work:** Include unit and integration tests with every change.
- **Own your mistakes:** We run blameless postmortems, and incidents are reviewed for what to learn, not who to blame.

## At 90 days

By three months, you should be able to ship features independently, take part in on-call, review code with confidence, and suggest improvements to our processes.

We're glad you're here. Questions are welcome, and so is pushback on how we do things.

People keep journals for reasons that are easy to name and hard to explain. A journal is a notebook, a stack of pages, or a file of dated entries. People write in one to remember and to understand, and sometimes just to get through a bad stretch. Writing slows life down enough to look at it.

Days blur and conversations fade. Even moments we swear we will never forget lose their edges. A journal keeps what memory lets go: the weather on an ordinary Tuesday, something said at dinner, what it felt like to wait for news. Writing these things down gives shape to a life that can feel scattered. Old entries can be startling to read, because the person in them is someone we used to be, more frightened or more hopeful, more certain or more confused. The pages show that we have changed.

Journals also help people make sense of what they feel now. Feelings arrive in pieces: anger with no known cause, sadness with no story, joy mixed with guilt, love tangled with fear. Writing sorts them out. A vague unease becomes a sentence, and the sentence sometimes becomes an insight. Many people find out what they think only after they see it on the page, so a journal helps produce thought as well as record it.

Writing that does not have to perform for anyone is freeing. Much of modern life is public or semi-public, and people edit themselves for employers, friends, family, and strangers online. A journal is one of the few places to be unpolished and contradictory: petty and generous, uncertain and dramatic, forgiving, all within the same hour. Nobody interrupts or asks for clarification or demands that feelings be reasonable. That privacy makes honesty possible.

Journaling can also be a way to endure loneliness, grief, illness, heartbreak, or confusion. The page takes what the world may not know how to hold. A journal cannot solve a crisis, but it can keep a person company through one and bear witness. Sometimes that gets someone through a day.

Ordinary lives fill most journals, and that is reason enough. The entries say: this happened, and I was here. I felt this. I wondered this. I changed.

History of the bicycle

The bicycle developed from experimental designs of the early 19th century into one of the most common forms of personal transport in the world. Steering, pedals, chain drive, and pneumatic tires were each added along the way, and the machine became a means of getting around as well as a sport and a pastime.

The earliest widely recognized predecessor was the dandy horse, also called the draisine, invented by the German baron Karl von Drais in 1817. It was built largely of wood and had two in-line wheels, the front one steerable, but no pedals. Riders pushed their feet against the ground. It showed the balance-and-steer principle that later designs relied on.

In the 1860s, inventors in France developed the velocipede, nicknamed the boneshaker for its rigid wooden or metal frame and iron-banded wheels, which made rough roads uncomfortable. Its pedals were mounted directly on the front wheel, so the rider no longer had to touch the ground to keep moving. Pierre Michaux and Pierre Lallement are often associated with its development and commercialization.

The high-wheel bicycle, or penny-farthing, became prominent in the 1870s. Because the pedals were fixed to the front wheel, a larger diameter meant more distance per pedal revolution, and the very large wheel gave greater speed. It was hard to mount and dangerous. Riders sat high above the ground and could be thrown forward in falls known as "headers."

The safety bicycle appeared in the 1880s, associated especially with John Kemp Starley and his 1885 Rover. It had two wheels of similar size, a chain drive to the rear wheel, and a lower center of gravity, which made it safer and more accessible than the penny-farthing. It set the basic form of the modern bicycle.

John Boyd Dunlop patented the pneumatic tire in 1888. Air-filled tires absorbed shocks from uneven road surfaces and improved comfort and speed. Together with diamond-frame construction, ball bearings, and better brakes, they made the bicycle practical for everyday use.

By the late 19th century, bicycles had become part of social and economic life in Europe and North America. They gave people more personal mobility and influenced road improvement movements. They also played a part in women's emancipation, since a bicycle offered independent transportation and encouraged changes in clothing and social conventions. In the 20th century, bicycles remained important for transport, sport, and industry. In the 21st they have drawn renewed attention in urban mobility, environmental policy, and public health.

# Backend Team Onboarding Guide

Welcome to the backend team. This guide covers what to do in your first weeks and how we work.

## 1. Your First Week

Start with environment setup. You need access to:

- Source code repositories
- CI/CD tools
- Cloud environments
- Monitoring and logging platforms
- Team communication channels
- Documentation systems
- Password and secrets management tools

Follow the setup documentation. If a step is unclear or broken, ask right away. Setup problems are common, and reporting them fixes the docs for the next hire.

Also book short intro meetings with your manager, your onboarding buddy, and the teammates you'll work with most. Ask who owns which services, how the team communicates, and what the current priorities are.

## 2. Understand the System

Backend systems tend to be distributed, with many pieces that depend on each other. Start by learning:

- Core services and their responsibilities
- Main data flows between services
- Datastores, queues, and third-party dependencies
- Deployment process and release cadence
- Key operational dashboards and alerts

You won't absorb all of it at once. Begin with the systems your team owns and work outward from there.

## 3. Development Workflow

Learn how the team works day to day:

- Branching and pull request process
- Coding standards and testing expectations
- Local development and debugging workflows
- How to run unit, integration, and end-to-end tests
- How changes move from development to production

Before you open your first PR, read a few recent ones. They show the team's norms on code quality, comments, and review speed.

## 4. Production Mindset

Backend engineers operate reliable systems as well as write code. Learn how the team handles:

- Logging and observability
- Incident response and escalation
- Rollbacks and safe deployments
- Performance, scalability, and cost awareness
- Security and data privacy requirements

When you make a change, check the failure modes, the monitoring, and the effect on downstream systems, along with whether the code is correct.

Start with small, low-risk changes, such as:

- Fixing a minor bug
- Improving documentation
- Adding or updating tests
- Making a small internal tooling improvement

These work well because you learn the codebase, the deployment pipeline, and the review process while the stakes stay low. Try to ship something small within your first two weeks.

Ask questions early and often. Code alone rarely gives you the context, and backend systems get complicated. Keep notes as you learn, especially on architecture, service ownership, and recurring team terms.

Onboarding is shared work. You stay curious and keep asking; the team backs you up.

# Westbrook University Announces Free Tuition for Students from Low-Income Families

**New "Westbrook Promise" program will cover full tuition for families earning under $75,000 beginning next fall**

WESTBROOK, Ohio — Westbrook University announced Tuesday that it will eliminate tuition for undergraduates from families earning less than $75,000 a year. Administrators say the change will let thousands of students attend who might otherwise be priced out.

The program, called the Westbrook Promise, takes effect with the incoming class next fall. It applies to all admitted students who are Ohio residents and meet the income threshold, and they stay eligible for four years as long as they maintain satisfactory academic progress.

"Talent is distributed equally across our communities, but opportunity is not," said university President Dr. Elena Marchetti at a press conference on campus. "No student who earns a place at Westbrook should have to turn it down because of the price tag. With this program, we are keeping a promise to the families in our region."

The university estimates that roughly 4,200 current and future students will qualify during the first year. The program is expected to cost approximately $38 million annually. It will be funded mainly through a $400 million endowment campaign launched two years ago, along with reallocated institutional aid and state grants.

Tuition at Westbrook currently stands at $14,800 per year for in-state students. Housing, meals, and books are not covered, though officials said students may still qualify for additional need-based aid for those costs.

Junior Marcus Delgado, who works two part-time jobs to cover his expenses, said the announcement came as a surprise. "I've thought about dropping out more than once because of the loans I was piling up," he said. "Knowing that students after me won't have to go through that is a big deal."

Dana Whitfield, director of the Ohio College Access Network, praised the decision but said tuition is only one part of college affordability. "Free tuition is a major step, but living costs often determine whether students finish," she said. "We hope Westbrook will continue to expand support in those areas."

Provost James Okafor said the school plans to study additional support for housing, food insecurity, and transportation over the next year.

Applications for the incoming class are open through March 1. Families can learn about eligibility and apply for the Westbrook Promise through the university's financial aid office or website.

The university also plans to host information sessions at high schools across the region this winter.

I used to think cooking was a skill some people were born with. They could walk into a kitchen, pull things off shelves and out of drawers, and put a meal on the table that looked like it cost them nothing. I approached it like a student arriving late to an exam, anxious and underprepared and sure I was about to be found out. Every mistake felt like proof that I did not belong there. It took me a long time to see that failing is how you learn to cook.

My first memorable failure was scrambled eggs. Eggs are supposed to be easy, which made it worse. I turned the heat too high and walked away for less than a minute. When I came back, the eggs were dry and rubbery, and brown in places eggs should never be brown. I ate them anyway, mostly out of embarrassment. Even then I noticed that I had learned something specific and physical: how fast food changes under harsh heat, and how little time separates soft curds from overcooked regret. A recipe could have told me "medium-low heat." The eggs told me what that meant.

More of the same followed. I oversalted a soup and found out that seasoning is a gradual conversation that runs from start to finish, so the end is too late to begin it. I baked cookies that spread into one giant glossy sheet, and I learned that butter has moods, that dough can be too warm, and that measurements matter more in baking than I wanted them to. I burned garlic maybe a dozen times before I respected how quickly fragrance turns to bitterness. Each mistake was irritating and sometimes expensive, and I remember every one. The meals that came together easily mostly faded.

Cooking resists abstraction. Cut onions unevenly and they cook unevenly. Crowd the pan and the vegetables steam instead of browning. Impatience shows up on the plate. It has made me pay closer attention to the ingredients and to myself, to what I do when I rush because I am hungry, when I improvise because I am proud, when I skip instructions because I want to believe instinct is enough. The kitchen can be humbling, and I find its honesty useful.

My idea of competence changed too. I once believed good cooks never made mistakes. Now I think good cooks know how to recover. They lower the heat, add acid, start over with less resentment, and keep tasting. I have ruined enough meals to know that one ruined meal is survivable, and that is where my confidence in the kitchen comes from, not from getting everything right.

Every scorched pan and collapsed cake sharpened my senses and made me less afraid. I still make mistakes. When dinner goes wrong now, I no longer take it as a verdict on me. I look at what to change.

**Heat Wave Strains State Power Grid as Officials Ask Residents to Conserve**

Energy officials are asking residents and businesses to cut back on electricity during the evening peak as a heat wave this week strains the state's power grid. Air conditioners are running nonstop in millions of homes.

Temperatures reached the upper 90s and topped 100 degrees in several inland communities for a third straight day. Overnight lows stayed unusually warm, so cooling demand stayed high around the clock. Grid operators said electricity use rose sharply Monday and Tuesday and came close to seasonal records.

"We are seeing exceptionally high demand driven by sustained extreme temperatures," the state's independent grid operator said in a statement. "At this time, the system remains stable, but conservation is critical to reduce stress on the grid during peak hours."

Officials asked consumers to limit nonessential use between late afternoon and early evening, when solar generation starts to fall but air-conditioning demand does not. They suggested raising thermostats a few degrees, putting off large appliances such as dishwashers and washing machines, and turning off lights that aren't needed.

Utilities were also working to keep overtaxed equipment from failing. In some areas, transformers and local distribution lines were under more pressure, which could cause isolated blackouts even if the broader grid kept operating normally. Utility crews were on heightened alert for equipment failures.

Emergency management officials warned that losing power could be especially dangerous for older adults, young children, and people with medical conditions. Cities and counties opened cooling centers in libraries, community centers, and other public buildings. Health agencies urged people to stay hydrated, avoid strenuous outdoor activity, and check on neighbors.

Utilities and policymakers are increasingly worried about how well the state's energy system will hold up as extreme weather becomes more frequent. Climate scientists have long warned that rising temperatures make prolonged periods of intense heat more likely. That kind of heat can drive electricity demand to records, threaten transmission equipment, and reduce the efficiency of some power plants.

Manufacturers and food retailers, which depend on uninterrupted electricity, said they were watching conditions closely. Some large industrial customers voluntarily cut their consumption under demand-response programs designed to ease pressure on the grid.

Forecasters said the hottest weather should last through at least midweek, followed by a modest cooldown. Until then, officials said, avoiding widespread outages may depend partly on whether residents heed the calls to conserve.

"This is a moment when small actions taken by millions of people can make a meaningful difference," the grid operator said.

# Judge Blocks $1.2 Billion Highway Expansion, Citing Flawed Environmental Review

**RIVERTON —** A state court judge on Tuesday halted a planned $1.2 billion expansion of Interstate 74, ruling that transportation officials failed to adequately study the project's effects on air quality and nearby wetlands.

In a 58-page decision, Judge Marianne Holloway of the Franklin County Superior Court found that the State Department of Transportation relied on outdated traffic projections and did not meaningfully consider alternatives to widening the 22-mile corridor from four lanes to eight.

"The agency's analysis treated its preferred outcome as a foregone conclusion," Holloway wrote. "The law requires a hard look at the consequences, not a justification after the fact."

The ruling grants an injunction that prohibits construction, land acquisition, and contractor awards until the department completes a new environmental impact statement. Work was scheduled to begin in March.

The lawsuit was filed last year by a coalition of residents, environmental groups, and the town of Millbrook, which argued the expansion would increase pollution near schools and destroy 140 acres of protected wetlands along the Tallow River.

"This is a victory for communities that were told their concerns didn't matter," said Dana Ortiz, a Millbrook resident and lead plaintiff. "We never opposed improving safety. We opposed a plan that ignored the evidence."

Transportation Secretary Glenn Whitaker said the department was disappointed and is weighing an appeal. "This corridor sees more than 90,000 vehicles a day and has one of the highest crash rates in the state," he said in a statement. "Delay carries real costs, both in safety and in dollars."

The department estimates a year's delay could add $60 million to the project's cost. Business groups, including the Riverton Chamber of Commerce, criticized the decision, saying the expansion was essential to relieving freight bottlenecks.

"Every day that road stays congested, we lose productivity and jobs," said chamber president Alan Brooks.

Opponents countered that the department's own data showed congestion would return within a decade of completion, a phenomenon researchers call induced demand. Holloway wrote that the agency "dismissed without analysis" studies suggesting wider highways often attract additional traffic.

The department can appeal, revise the study, or look at alternatives such as added transit service, targeted safety upgrades, or a smaller expansion.

"A new review could take 18 months or longer," said Priya Natarajan, a land-use law professor at Riverton State University. "But if it's done thoroughly, it may produce a project that survives challenge."

The department has 30 days to file an appeal.

**Hildegard of Bingen** (1098–1179), also called Saint Hildegard and the Sibyl of the Rhine, was a German Benedictine abbess, composer, mystic, writer, and polymath of the High Middle Ages. She is one of the earliest composers in the Western tradition whose life is well documented, and one of the few medieval women whose music survives in quantity.

Hildegard was born in Bermersheim vor der Höhe, in the Rhineland, and was dedicated to the religious life at an early age. Jutta von Sponheim educated her in a monastic setting, and she later became leader of the community at Disibodenberg. In the 1150s she founded her own convent at Rupertsberg near Bingen, and later a daughter house at Eibingen. Besides running these communities, she wrote visionary theology, medical and scientific treatises, and a large body of letters, and she composed liturgical music.

Her best-known collection of songs is the *Symphonia armoniae celestium revelationum* (“Symphony of the Harmony of Celestial Revelations”), which contains more than 70 pieces: antiphons, responsories, hymns, sequences, and other chants for the Divine Office and the Mass. The texts are usually in Latin. They draw on the imagery of her visions and often celebrate the Virgin Mary, the saints, and the virtues.

Her best-known dramatic work is the *Ordo Virtutum* (“Play of the Virtues”), a sacred morality play and one of the earliest surviving musical dramas. The Virtues sing against the Devil, who speaks but never sings, which fits the medieval association of music with divine order. The play was probably performed within the convent.

Hildegard’s music is often more expansive than typical Gregorian chant, with wide melodic ranges and ornate, soaring lines. It rests on the plainchant tradition but is highly individual, and its melodies often stress emotional and spiritual elevation. Text and melody are closely tied, and musical gestures frequently mirror the imagery of the words.

After the Middle Ages her music fell into relative obscurity. It was revived in the 20th century through scholarship and performance, and she is now often ranked among the most significant composers of medieval Europe. In 2012 Pope Benedict XVI canonized her and declared her a Doctor of the Church.

The Rosetta Stone is a granodiorite stele inscribed with a decree issued in 196 BCE, under Ptolemy V Epiphanes, ruler of the Ptolemaic Kingdom in Egypt. The inscription is written in three scripts, and that made the stone the key to deciphering ancient Egyptian writing.

The same text appears in Ancient Greek, Demotic, and Egyptian hieroglyphs. Scholars could read Greek, but Demotic and hieroglyphs had long been unreadable. By comparing the three versions, researchers slowly worked out the meaning and structure of Egyptian writing, and the stone became central to the beginnings of Egyptology.

The decree came from a council of priests at Memphis. It affirmed the royal cult of Ptolemy V and listed the honors granted to him. Decrees like this were usually displayed in temples in several scripts so that different readers could follow them: hieroglyphs for formal and religious use, Demotic for everyday administration, and Greek for the Hellenistic ruling elite.

French soldiers found the stone in 1799, during Napoleon's campaign in Egypt, near the town of Rosetta (modern Rashid) in the Nile Delta. They were working on the fortifications of Fort Julien. After the French were defeated in Egypt, the Capitulation of Alexandria in 1801 made the stone British property, and it was taken to Britain.

It has been in the British Museum in London since 1802 and remains one of the museum's most visited objects. Calls for its return to Egypt have also made it part of the wider debate over cultural heritage and repatriation.

Decipherment was slow. Thomas Young identified relationships between the Greek and Demotic texts and made progress on some hieroglyphic signs. Jean-François Champollion made the decisive breakthrough in 1822, when he demonstrated that hieroglyphs combined phonetic and symbolic elements. That let scholars read ancient Egyptian texts more broadly.

The stone is incomplete, and parts of the original stele are missing. Still, substantial portions of all three versions of the decree survive. Today "Rosetta Stone" is also used metaphorically for any key to understanding a previously obscure subject.

# Runbook: Restarting a Stuck Message Queue

## Purpose
How to restart a message queue service that is stuck or not processing messages. Written for on-call engineers and operators handling incidents in production or lower environments.

## Symptoms
Use this runbook if you see any of the following:
- Queue depth is rising and not draining
- Producers are publishing but consumers receive nothing
- The queue management UI or API does not respond
- Error rates are high, or connections time out, or retries keep failing
- The queue process is running but health checks fail

## Preconditions
Before restarting, confirm:
- You can reach the host, container platform, or orchestration tool
- You know the queue name, service name, and environment
- No active incident involves storage, network, or dependent services
- You know whether the queue is clustered and whether failover is available

## Safety Checks
1. Assess impact
   - Identify the affected applications and users.
   - Decide whether backlog growth during the restart is tolerable.

2. Capture current state
   - Record queue depth, consumer count, producer rate, and error logs.
   - Save screenshots or command output from the monitoring dashboards.

3. Verify persistence
   - If durability or replication is required, confirm messages have it.
   - If the queue is non-durable, note that messages may be lost.

4. Rule out a root cause
   - Check for a full disk, memory exhaustion, expired certificates, or a downstream outage. A restart may only help temporarily if one of these is the cause.

## Restart Procedure
1. Notify stakeholders
   - Announce the restart in the incident channel, with expected impact and estimated duration.

2. Pause or drain traffic if you can
   - Stop producers or consumers temporarily if your platform supports it.
   - In clustered setups, redirect traffic to healthy nodes first.

3. Restart the service
   - systemd hosts: `sudo systemctl restart <service-name>`
   - Containers: restart the pod, task, or container through the orchestrator
   - Clustered brokers: restart only the affected node unless a broader action is approved

4. Monitor startup
   - Watch the service logs for a clean initialization.
   - Confirm health checks pass and management endpoints respond.

## Validation
After the restart, confirm:
- The queue service is healthy
- Queue depth is stable or falling
- Consumers reconnect
- Producers can publish without errors
- Latency, retries, and dead-letter messages show no unusual spikes

## Rollback / Escalation
Escalate immediately if:
- The service fails to start
- Queue depth keeps growing after the restart
- Messages appear lost or corrupted
- More than one node shows the same problem

If the restart does not fix it, contact the messaging/platform team and attach the logs, metrics, timestamps, and actions you took.

## Post-Incident
- Document the timeline, cause, and recovery steps
- Create follow-up tasks for root cause analysis
- Check whether alerts, dashboards, or autoscaling thresholds need adjusting

The Great Molasses Flood, also called the Boston Molasses Disaster, happened on January 15, 1919, in the North End of Boston, Massachusetts. A storage tank owned by the United States Industrial Alcohol Company burst and sent a wave of molasses through the surrounding streets. It killed 21 people and injured about 150.

The tank stood near Commercial Street. It was about 50 feet (15 m) high and 90 feet (27 m) across, and it held roughly 2.3 million gallons (8.7 million liters) of molasses. The company used molasses to make industrial alcohol, which went into munitions during and after World War I. When the tank ruptured, the molasses surged through the neighborhood. Contemporary reports put the wave at up to 25 feet (7.6 m) high and about 35 miles per hour (56 km/h), though the exact figures are still debated.

Buildings were knocked off their foundations, and the supports of an elevated railway were damaged. Horses, wagons, and people were caught in the molasses. It coated the streets, the debris, and the victims, which made rescue slow and hard. Firefighters, police officers, soldiers, and residents all helped with the rescue and cleanup. Syrup covered the area for weeks, and later accounts say people in Boston could smell molasses on warm days for years afterward.

Many lawsuits were filed against the company. After a long legal process, investigators concluded that the tank had been poorly built and inadequately tested. Evidence suggested the steel walls were too thin and that the tank had leaked even before it failed. The case is an early example of corporate liability, and it helped lead to stricter standards for engineering oversight, construction, and safety in the United States.

The flood has been the subject of books, documentaries, and local folklore. People remember it for the deaths and for how strange it was.
