# My First Risotto

The first meal I cooked for anyone besides myself was risotto, and I picked it for a bad reason: I wanted to impress someone. I'd read that risotto was hard, which at twenty-two seemed like an argument for making it. What I served was a gluey, undersalted paste with rice that was still crunchy in the center. My guest ate three bites, said "interesting," and asked if we could order pizza.

I was mortified. I was also curious, which surprised me. How could the rice crunch and turn to glue at the same time? Those two things should have canceled each other out. That question did more to make me a cook than any dinner I've pulled off since.

A bad essay can be defended and a flawed argument can be dressed up, but a chicken breast is either cooked through or it isn't. Nobody gives partial credit for effort in a kitchen, and I find that clarifying. When a sauce breaks, I can usually name the reason: the heat was too high, I added the butter too fast, I walked away to answer a text. The feedback is immediate and physical, and there's no arguing with it.

Over the years my failures have turned into a private curriculum. I found out about the Maillard reaction by steaming mushrooms I meant to brown. I'd crowded the pan, and they sat in their own gray liquid. I learned that salt isn't a garnish by eating a whole season of bland soups. I scorched garlic often enough that the bitter, acrid smell now sets off something like an alarm in my body. My actual smoke alarm and I have an understanding, too, and it has taught me more about preheating cast iron than any book.

Early on, every mistake felt like a verdict on me. Now it feels like information. When the bread comes out dense, I don't think *I'm a bad baker*; I think *the dough was probably underproofed, or the kitchen was cold.* Somewhere along the way, shame turned into troubleshooting.

The best cooks I know aren't the ones who rarely fail. They fail without making a scene. My grandmother fed a family of nine, and once she dropped an entire pan of roasted potatoes on the floor, scooped up the ones that hadn't rolled under the stove, and called the rest "extra crispy." She meant it. Dinner was still happening.

Not long ago, I made risotto again. I stood at the stove for forty minutes, stirring, tasting, adding stock a ladle at a time, until I could tell the moment the grains went creamy but still had a little resistance. It wasn't perfect. It needed more lemon. But it was good, and I knew exactly why.

Standing there, I thought about that first batch, the paste and the crunch and the polite "interesting," and I was grateful for it.

**Only Grocery Store in Maple Ridge to Close, Leaving Residents Facing Long Trips for Basics**

**MAPLE RIDGE, June 12** — Maple Ridge Market, the town's only grocery store, will close June 30, owner Daniel Harper said. The next nearest supermarket is nearly 25 miles away.

The market has been open for more than three decades and is the community's primary source for groceries, fresh produce, dairy products and over-the-counter medications.

Harper blamed rising costs, supply chain problems and declining sales.

"We've done everything we could to keep the store open," Harper said in an interview Tuesday. "But higher wholesale prices, utility bills, and the difficulty of competing with larger chains have taken a real toll. This wasn't an easy decision."

Neighbors in the town of 1,800 also used the store to catch up on local news and check in on one another. Residents say the closure will fall hardest on older adults, low-income families and people without reliable transportation.

"This store is a lifeline," said longtime resident Martha Jennings, 72. "Not everyone can just drive to the city whenever they need milk or bread. A lot of people here depend on this place."

Town officials say they are looking at temporary fixes: partnering with nearby food banks, organizing volunteer ride programs and encouraging mobile food vendors to stop in Maple Ridge regularly. Mayor Carla Ruiz called the closure "a serious challenge" and said the town is already in discussions with regional agencies and local nonprofits.

"We know this will create hardship for many families," Ruiz said. "Our priority is making sure no one in Maple Ridge is left without access to basic necessities."

Twelve jobs will go with the store, in a town where work is scarce. Harper said he hopes some employees can find jobs in neighboring communities, though he acknowledged the transition will be difficult.

Residents have started circulating petitions and discussing cooperative ownership models, hoping to bring a grocery option back to town eventually. Some are calling for state assistance with what advocates describe as a growing "rural food access" problem affecting small communities across the region.

For now, the shelves at Maple Ridge Market are thinning as customers make what may be their last trips through the aisles.

# History of printing in Korea

The **history of printing in Korea** begins before the mid-8th century and includes some of the earliest known woodblock prints and the oldest surviving book printed with movable metal type. Most Korean printing was done within Buddhist and state institutions, and it was used to preserve religious, historical, and administrative texts.

## Early woodblock printing

Woodblock printing reached Korea through contact with Tang China. The *Mugujeonggwang Great Dharani Sutra*, discovered in 1966 inside a pagoda at Bulguksa temple, is generally dated to before 751 in the Unified Silla period. It is among the oldest surviving printed texts in the world.

During the Goryeo dynasty (918–1392), royal and monastic patrons supported a large printing industry. The *Tripitaka Koreana*, a complete Buddhist canon, was carved on more than 80,000 woodblocks between 1236 and 1251, partly as an act of devotion during the Mongol invasions. The blocks are kept at Haeinsa temple and were inscribed on the UNESCO Memory of the World Register in 2007.

## Metal movable type

Goryeo printers developed movable type cast in metal, probably in the early 13th century. Records suggest that the *Sangjeong Gogeum Yemun* was printed with metal type around 1234, though no copy survives. The oldest extant book printed with movable metal type is the *Jikji*, a collection of Zen Buddhist teachings printed at Heungdeoksa temple in Cheongju in 1377. Its second volume is held by the Bibliothèque nationale de France and was added to the Memory of the World Register in 2001.

# Runbook: Restarting a Stuck Message Queue

**Purpose:** Restore message processing when a queue has stopped consuming or is backing up.
**Audience:** On-call engineers
**Estimated time:** 15-30 minutes

---

## 1. Confirm the Problem

Before acting, verify the queue is actually stuck rather than slow.

- Check queue depth: is it growing steadily?
- Check consumer count: are consumers connected?
- Check message age: is the oldest message unusually old?
- Review consumer logs for errors, deadlocks, or repeated retries.

If consumers are healthy and depth is falling, wait and monitor instead.

## 2. Assess Impact

- Identify upstream producers and downstream consumers.
- Notify the incident channel that you are investigating.
- Determine whether messages are safe to delay or must be preserved at all costs.

## 3. Capture Diagnostic Data

Do this **before** restarting, since a restart destroys evidence.

- Export queue metrics and screenshots of dashboards.
- Save consumer logs from the last 30 minutes.
- Take a thread dump or heap snapshot from a stuck consumer if possible.
- Note the current queue depth and oldest message timestamp.

## 4. Check for a Poison Message

A single malformed message often blocks processing.

- Inspect the head of the queue.
- If the same message is redelivered repeatedly, move it to the dead-letter queue (DLQ) manually.
- Resume consumers and check whether processing recovers.

## 5. Restart Consumers First

This is the least disruptive option.

1. Stop the consumer service gracefully.
2. Wait for in-flight messages to be acknowledged or timed out.
3. Start consumers one at a time.
4. Watch consumer count and depth for 5 minutes.

## 6. Restart the Broker (Only If Necessary)

If consumers restart cleanly but the queue remains stuck:

1. Confirm messages are persisted to disk (durable queues).
2. Announce the restart in the incident channel.
3. In clustered setups, restart one node at a time and wait for it to rejoin and sync.
4. Never restart all nodes simultaneously.
5. Verify the queue and its bindings reappear after restart.

## 7. Verify Recovery

- Queue depth is decreasing.
- Consumers are connected and acknowledging messages.
- Error rates have returned to baseline.
- No unexpected messages landed in the DLQ.
- Send a test message end to end.

## 8. Handle Backlog

Large backlogs can overwhelm consumers after recovery.

- Scale consumers temporarily if needed.
- Throttle producers if downstream systems are strained.
- Check for duplicates if your system uses at-least-once delivery.

## 9. Follow Up

- Post a resolution update in the incident channel.
- Record the timeline, root cause, and actions taken.
- File tickets for permanent fixes, such as better poison message handling, alerting on consumer lag, or retry limits.
- Schedule a postmortem if customer impact occurred.

---

## Escalation

If the queue is still stuck after a broker restart, or data loss is suspected, escalate to the platform team lead immediately. Do not purge the queue without explicit approval.

# Harlan Falls loses its only grocery store

**HARLAN FALLS —** The automatic doors at Miller's Market slid shut for the last time Saturday evening. The town of 2,100 now has no grocery store for the first time in 71 years.

Owner Dale Miller, 64, flipped the sign to "Closed" at 6 p.m. while about three dozen residents stood in the parking lot. Some brought flowers, and many said nothing.

"I tried everything I could think of," Miller said, his voice catching. "The numbers just stopped working."

Miller inherited the store from his father in 1994. He said rising wholesale costs, higher energy bills, and a discount supercenter 28 miles away had steadily cut into his margins. In March the refrigeration system failed, and the replacement estimate came to $85,000.

"You can't ask a store this size to absorb that," he said. "I'd have been working just to pay off a freezer."

Residents without reliable transportation are hit hardest. County census data shows nearly one in five Harlan Falls households includes someone over 65, and many of them no longer drive.

"I'm 82. I'm not driving to Dunmore on the highway," said Ruth Eckhart, who has shopped at Miller's weekly since the 1960s. "My son says he'll take me every other Saturday, but what do I eat in between?"

Mayor Connie Reyes said the town council will hold an emergency meeting Thursday. Options include a volunteer delivery program through the senior center and a possible shuttle to the supercenter. She has also contacted the state agriculture department about grants for rural food access.

"A grocery store isn't just a business," Reyes said. "It's where you find out who's in the hospital, who needs help, whose kid just got into college. We're going to lose that, too."

The Gas-N-Go on Route 9 sells milk, bread, and canned goods, but Miller's customers say its prices run 30 to 40 percent higher. The weekly farmers market has produce but no staples, and it operates only from June through September.

Some residents are exploring a community-owned cooperative store, which has brought groceries back to other rural towns. A planning group meets at the library next week.

Marcus Webb, a teenager who worked the register at Miller's for two years, stayed after the crowd left. "It was my first job," he said. "Everybody knew my name."

Miller said he has no immediate plans beyond cleaning out the building. The property is listed for sale.

"I just hope somebody builds something here," he said, looking back at the dark windows. "This town deserves it."
